question: to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:

The video games sector is one of Europe’s most innovative cultural and creative sectors. It employs talented, highly skilled people and promotes technological progress, digital skills and cross-border growth. There are some 5 900 games studios in Europe, many of which are SMEs or independent developers. The European Parliament and the Council have recognised how strategically important the sector is for innovation, cultural diversity and the creative economy. The sector’s growth has been supported by innovative business models, in particular the freeto-play model, where games are free and revenues are based on in-game currencies such as coins, diamonds and precious stones. These can either be earned through playing the game or purchased with real money. Operators in the industry have expressed concern that the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) currently under consideration could require the price of virtual products to be displayed in euro every time they are used. This could lead to price confirmations being shown repeatedly during the same gaming session, undermine the user experience and make European gaming companies less competitive on the global market. 1.
How does the Commission intend to ensure that, in practice, the DFA does not make the pay-to-play model unworkable or undermine the competitiveness of the sector?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that future regulation is proportionate, evidence-based and compatible with existing EU legislation, in particular in the light of the Regulatory Scrutiny Board’s negative assessment of the way in which preparations for the DFA are being made?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) EU consumer legislation1 requires traders to ensure price transparency towards consumers. The Commission considers that price transparency requirements apply also in cases where traders, such as video games providers, introduce in-game currencies as intermediate means that consumers must use for purchasing in-game virtual items2. Member States’ consumer authorities acting within the Consumer Protection Co-operation (CPC) network have also endorsed this interpretation of EU law in the CPC Network’s Key Principles on In-game Virtual currencies. Enforcement of existing EU consumer legislation being a priority, the Commission continues to facilitate discussions between the CPC Network and the video game industry to uphold existing EU consumer rights3. The upcoming Digital Fairness Act4 (DFA) will address identified consumer protection gaps and problematic features in digital products and services5, including video games. The impact assessment examines if action is needed on specific topics, including clarification of the existing price transparency rules when virtual currencies are deployed, e.g. through indicating the price both in virtual and real currency. It assesses various approaches, including coregulation, to frame possible measures. The impact assessment process includes an examination by the Regulatory Scrutiny Board. By clarifying consumer protection rules, the DFA will facilitate enforcement, provide greater legal certainty, a more level playing field and more harmonisation for traders. It will also include important simplification elements, such as reduction of consumer information requirements for contracts concerning in-app purchases, whilst maintaining the price transparency principle.
1 See Articles 5 and 6 of Directive 2011/83/EU on consumer rights,

http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/83/oj; Article 7 of Directive 2005/29/EC on Unfair Commercial Practices, http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj. 2 See Section 4.2.9 of Commission Notice – Guidance on the interpretation and application of Directive 2005/29/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council concerning unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices in the internal market, OJ C 526, 29.12.2021, pp. 1–129. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_831. 4 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/consultations/commission-launches-open-consultation-forthcomingdigital-fairness-act. 5 See Commission Staff Working Document ‘Fitness Check of EU consumer law on digital fairness’ of 3.10.2024, SWD(2024) 230 final.
